s1-000-fd2ac3fbd51cf420.wav.text: Episode two of the autograd engine.

s1-001-900065d6b76fa02c.wav.text: Last time we built the local rules, one per operation.

s1-002-cf6b4d3a7519f065.wav.text: Today we run them, and the entire content of this episode is the word order.

s1-003-54f177b7e2cb8f56.wav.text: Because the local rules are individually correct and collectively useless until they execute in the right sequence.

s2-000-8d9da9defe31c00d.wav.text: Here is the constraint, and it is the only thing you have to hold onto.

s2-001-794d1af5cfa49a2f.wav.text: A node hands gradient to its children.

s2-002-7aab5f59768dbd73.wav.text: But that node's own gradient is a sum over all of its consumers, and the sum is only complete once every consumer has contributed.

s2-003-b9fc02f5e1515316.wav.text: So if you run a node too early, it pushes a partial sum downstream, and every node below it inherits the mistake.

s2-005-f3aa5e99a7fe1d45.wav.text: Every node strictly after all of its consumers.

s2-006-7d555dc793c115f2.wav.text: Which is a topological sort of the graph, reversed.

s2-007-3b5e298b92932ba6.wav.text: And it is worth naming three orders that look plausible and are not it.

s2-008-a2922fd493e2ca79.wav.text: The order you created the nodes in is not it.

s2-009-d971559e4bed49ad.wav.text: Sorting by depth is not it.

s2-010-4379f4daae60c473.wav.text: And the order that naive recursion happens to visit in is not it either, though it comes closest.

s2-011-ef56b40a6d4e06c3.wav.text: If you have ever written a build system, this is the same constraint.

s2-012-49d94454ca5e2361.wav.text: Compile a dependency before the things that depend on it.

s2-013-765f02e730667107.wav.text: Reverse mode autodiff is make, run backwards.

s3-000-8bfe5997563cf303.wav.text: The smallest graph that can catch you is the diamond. x feeds two different operations. a is two x. b is tanh of x.

s3-002-cb510f955ac328a6.wav.text: Watch the dashed arrows and their numbers. y runs first.

s3-003-4f382bf13532bf20.wav.text: It pushes into a, then into b.

s3-006-c76057f3c080dc93.wav.text: And only now is x's gradient complete.

s3-007-5df4d38bda314b94.wav.text: Now imagine we ran x after a but before b. x would push a gradient downstream that is missing the entire tanh path.

s3-008-09253007f8d843ba.wav.text: In this tiny graph x is a leaf, so nothing is downstream and the damage is contained to a wrong final answer.

s3-009-64df0ad2f7db5a7e.wav.text: In a real network x is a hidden activation with fifty layers under it, and every one of them is now wrong by a factor nobody can see.

s4-000-5794d550ead20524.wav.text: Here is the traversal, and it is worth reading slowly because the two phase trick is not obvious the first time.

s4-001-52d8e3ddd6527f22.wav.text: Each stack entry is a node plus a boolean saying whether its children have already been pushed.

s4-003-69aa2914909921cc.wav.text: If the flag is set, the children are already emitted, so this node is safe to append.

s4-004-44d0905b9052ce20.wav.text: If the flag is clear, this is the first time we have reached the node.

s4-005-ad3fb683948730eb.wav.text: Mark it seen, so a diamond cannot enqueue it twice.

s4-006-cc0e14fc967963d4.wav.text: Then push the node back with the flag set, and after that push its children.

s4-007-9bce9e2f47fb0f69.wav.text: The stack is last in first out, so the children pop before the node does, which is exactly the post order we want.

s4-008-84464eadf615691e.wav.text: The result is a list where every node appears after all of its children.

s4-009-eebddc1ae30e42ae.wav.text: Reverse that list and every node appears after all of its consumers, which is the constraint from two scenes ago.

s5-000-118309b7abfb1242.wav.text: And here is why we did it with an explicit stack rather than recursion.

s5-001-5caba4ef93571fe3.wav.text: The recursive version is three lines and it is correct, and it dies.

s5-002-9966d4f32ad155d2.wav.text: Take a single value and multiply it by a constant twenty thousand times.

s5-003-d3178420b5243552.wav.text: That is a chain twenty thousand nodes deep, which is not an unusual depth once you unroll even a small network to scalars.

s5-004-054e8f26ecf1dc98.wav.text: Python's default recursion limit is one thousand.

s5-006-7a9503e42738fdd0.wav.text: The iterative one does not, and there is a test in the suite that does exactly this, because it is the kind of limit you would rather find in continuous integration than during a training run.

s6-000-2da1b06b9acb6a92.wav.text: And here is the whole backward pass.

s6-003-257b09ad02d602ae.wav.text: Zero every gradient, because calling backward twice on the same graph must not double the numbers.

s6-004-072fc21f5733a424.wav.text: Set the root's gradient to one, which is the seed, and the only derivative in the entire system that you write down by hand.

s6-005-8c50130f2c57179e.wav.text: Then walk the order in reverse and call each node's closure exactly once.

s6-007-645a62e9ba9ac064.wav.text: Everything else in this episode was explaining why line six says reversed.

s7-000-ac895be8f53a6e01.wav.text: There is a design decision hiding in line three that is worth pulling out, because you will meet the other side of it constantly.

s7-001-fb86e25cb02bff83.wav.text: This engine zeroes gradients at the start of backward.

s7-003-5703f9955caa5b41.wav.text: PyTorch accumulates across calls and makes you call zero grad yourself.

s7-004-a68aa38ae549efe5.wav.text: That choice is why forgetting zero grad is the single most common beginner bug in PyTorch.

s7-005-2531a3d558ecdc09.wav.text: It is also why gradient accumulation across micro batches is completely free there.

s7-006-b6bddacd47c1fd78.wav.text: Call backward four times, step once, and you have trained on a batch four times larger than fits in memory.

s7-008-1951331b84b1e9bb.wav.text: But an engine has to pick one and say so, because the two behave identically right up until they do not.

s8-000-d3ea2ca02f6731ad.wav.text: And to make the point concrete, here is the diamond evaluated numerically.

s8-001-10b5382c93ecfd42.wav.text: The derivative of two x times tanh x, at x equals one point five.

s8-002-60a2ec5a8cfd85c7.wav.text: Reverse topological order gives two point nine two nine.

s8-003-f15a74ce3001ec51.wav.text: The analytic answer, worked out on paper, gives two point nine two nine.

s8-004-51d288dd7df5fdd2.wav.text: Insertion order gives one point nine nine five.

s8-005-be47a586bd97c406.wav.text: Look at that third bar for a moment.

s8-007-202aa818346dad8e.wav.text: It is the right order of magnitude.

s8-009-69c4850cb9f6e121.wav.text: It is thirty two percent wrong and nothing anywhere raised an exception.

s8-010-3c18955331464423.wav.text: This is what I mean when I say autograd bugs do not announce themselves, and it is why the gradcheck from episode one is not optional infrastructure.

s9-001-d9672414c62587cd.wav.text: A node may push gradient only after every one of its consumers has pushed into it.

s9-002-7c591a3b0825069c.wav.text: That ordering is a topological sort, reversed, and it is not insertion order and not depth.

s9-003-eee08994a798f1ed.wav.text: Implement the traversal with an explicit two phase stack, because a scalar unrolled network is tens of thousands of nodes deep and recursion will not survive it.

s9-004-cb99737ab5884330.wav.text: Backward itself is one traversal, zero everything, seed the root with one, run in reverse.

s9-005-da4d2644092d3851.wav.text: And the zeroing policy is a genuine design choice where PyTorch went the other way, which is the entire reason zero grad exists.

s9-006-a77eb7cfd6dc76e1.wav.text: Skip this and the wrong order will not crash.

s9-007-5499a0d37da51d62.wav.text: It will hand you a plausible number that is a third too small, and train a slightly worse model forever.

s9-008-06306db8ec1fe0ed.wav.text: Next episode is the hard one.

s9-009-48762234dae9c8ed.wav.text: The same engine, on arrays, where broadcasting turns a one line convenience in the forward pass into a summation you have to get exactly right on the way back.
